'''David Marcelo Sabatini''' (born 1968) is an American scientist and a former professor of biology at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT). From 2002 to 2021, he was a member of the [[Whitehead Institute|Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research]]. He was also an investigator of the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]] from 2008 to 2021 and was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2016. He is known for his contributions in the areas of cell signaling and cancer metabolism, most notably the co-discovery of [[mTOR]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Sabatini DM, Erdjument-Bromage H, Lui M, Tempst P, Snyder SH | title = RAFT1: a mammalian protein that binds to FKBP12 in a rapamycin-dependent fashion and is homologous to yeast TORs | journal = Cell | volume = 78 | issue = 1 | pages = 35–43 | date = July 1994 | pmid = 7518356 | doi = 10.1016/0092-8674(94)90570-3 | s2cid = 33647539 }}</ref>

In 2021 and 2022, Sabatini was fired from the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and resigned his positions at the Whitehead Institute and MIT, following allegations of [[sexual harassment]].<ref name="Wadman-2021"/><ref name="science2022"/><ref name="nytimes"/> Sabatini denies the allegations. In October 2026, Sabatini won a defamation lawsuit against his accuser, Kristin Knouse, who was ordered to pay him over $6 million in damages.<ref>{{cite news
 |last=Arsenault
 |first=Mark
 |title=M.I.T. Scientist Wins $6 Million in Sexual Harassment Defamation Suit
 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/us/mit-scientist-sexual-harassment-defamation-lawsuit-david-sabatini.html
 |work=The New York Times
 |date=October 16, 2026
 |access-date=October 19, 2026
}}</ref>

==Biography==
Sabatini was born in 1968<ref name="q483">{{cite web | title=David M. Sabatini, 12th Frontiers of Knowledge Award in Biology and Biomedicine | website=Premios Fronteras | date=January 15, 2025 | url=https://www.frontiersofknowledgeawards-fbbva.es/galardonados/david-sabatini-2/ | access-date=October 30, 2026}}</ref><ref name="k375">{{cite web | title=MTOR Is a Big Boss With the Capacity to Listen. In Prague, We Started by Sterilizing Distilled Water | website=2. lékařská fakulta Univerzity Karlovy | date=October 8, 2025 | url=https://www.lf2.cuni.cz/clanky/mtor-is-a-big-boss-with-the-capacity-to-listen-in-prague-we-started-by-sterilizing-distilled | access-date=October 30, 2026}}</ref> and raised in [[New York City]] to [[David D. Sabatini]] and Zulema Sabatini, both [[Argentine]] immigrants from [[Buenos Aires]]. He obtained his B.S. from [[Brown University]] followed by both his MD and his Ph.D. at [[Johns Hopkins School of Medicine]],<ref>{{cite thesis| title=Control of translation by a novel, rapamycin-sensitive signaling pathway | type=PhD thesis|year=1997|publisher=Johns Hopkins University| last=Sabatini | first=David Marcelo| url=https://catalyst.library.jhu.edu/permalink/01JHU_INST/b9593h/alma991015839989707861|access-date=October 30, 2026}}</ref> where he worked in the lab of [[Solomon H. Snyder]]. He joined the Whitehead Institute as a [[Whitehead Fellow]] in 1997, the same year he graduated from Johns Hopkins.<ref name="Viegas-2017" /> In 2002 he became an assistant professor at MIT and a Member of the Whitehead Institute. He was promoted to tenured professor in 2006.

Sabatini's father, David D. Sabatini, is a cell biologist and [[professor emeritus]] at [[New York University]]. His younger brother, [[Bernardo L. Sabatini]], is a neuroscientist and professor at [[Harvard Medical School]].<ref name="Viegas-2017" /><ref name="hhmi">{{cite web|url=https://www.hhmi.org/bulletin/spring-2013/science-their-blood|title=Science in their Blood|last1=Ware|first1=Lauren|date=2013|website=HHMI Bulletin|publisher=Howard Hughes Medical Institute|access-date=April 5, 2017}}</ref>

Sabatini is the scientific founder of Navitor,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.navitorpharma.com/about/founder.html |title=Navitor Pharmaceuticals |access-date=September 12, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171114165812/http://www.navitorpharma.com/about/founder.html |archive-date=November 14, 2017 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Raze Therapeutics,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://razetx.com/about/founders/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161201144252/http://razetx.com/about/founders/ | archive-date=December 1, 2016| url-status=dead |title=Founders|access-date=May 4, 2022|website=Raze Therapeutics}}</ref> and KSQ Therapeutics.<ref>[https://ksqtx.com/ Kendall Square Therapeutics]</ref>

===Misconduct allegations and litigation===
{{anchor|Allegations of sexual misconduct}}
In 2021, the [[Whitehead Institute]], where Sabatini led a research laboratory, commissioned Hinckley Allen to investigate allegations of sexual harassment and inappropriate laboratory conduct. Central to the investigation were allegations by Kristin Knouse, a biologist leading her own Whitehead laboratory.<ref name="Knouse-MIT-bio">{{cite web |title=Kristin Knouse |url=https://ki.mit.edu/people/faculty/kristin-knouse |website=Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research |publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology |access-date=October 30, 2026}}</ref> She and Sabatini had begun a sexual relationship in 2018. It ended in early 2020 after he told her he was involved with biologist Lena Pernas, whom he married that December. In late 2020, Knouse accused Sabatini of sexual harassment in complaints to Whitehead director [[Ruth Lehmann]] and encouraged other researchers to complain. Sabatini maintained that the relationship was consensual.<ref name="Globe-Spotlight-2023-2">{{cite news |last1=Irons |first1=Meghan E. |last2=Arsenault |first2=Mark |last3=Wen |first3=Patricia |title=A broken bond, a shaken citadel of science |url=https://apps.bostonglobe.com/metro/investigations/spotlight/2023/01/fallen-star/shaken-citadel-science/ |work=The Boston Globe |date=January 28, 2023 |access-date=October 30, 2026}}</ref>

The Hinckley Allen investigation concluded that Sabatini had violated institutional policies and fostered a sexualized laboratory environment.<ref name="Globe-Spotlight-2023-2"/> A 2023 ''[[The Boston Globe|Boston Globe]]'' Spotlight investigation documented poor judgment and policy violations but found that investigators "may have drawn overly severe conclusions in some areas."<ref name="Globe-Spotlight-2023-1">{{cite news |last1=Arsenault |first1=Mark |last2=Irons |first2=Meghan E. |last3=Wen |first3=Patricia |title=Fate and the fallen star |url=https://apps.bostonglobe.com/metro/investigations/spotlight/2023/01/fallen-star/fall-of-david-sabatini/ |work=The Boston Globe |date=January 28, 2023 |access-date=October 30, 2026}}</ref>

In August 2021, Sabatini was forced to resign from Whitehead and dismissed by the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]], which funded his research.<ref name="Wadman-2021">{{cite news |last=Wadman |first=Meredith |title=HHMI fires prominent biologist for sexual harassment |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/hhmi-fires-prominent-biologist-sexual-harassment |work=Science |publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science |date=August 21, 2021}}</ref> He disputed the fairness of the Hinckley Allen investigation and sued Knouse, Whitehead and Lehmann that October.<ref name="Murphy-2025">{{cite news |last=Murphy |first=Pat |title=Judge: ex-lab director can sue accuser for defamation |url=https://masslawyersweekly.com/2025/11/20/defamation-lawsuit-whitehead-institute/ |work=Massachusetts Lawyers Weekly |date=November 20, 2025 |access-date=October 30, 2026}}</ref> Knouse counterclaimed in December, alleging sexual harassment and retaliation.<ref name="Fox-2021">{{cite news |last=Fox |first=Jeremy C. |title=Lawsuit alleges MIT professor 'groomed' young women, ran 'sexually charged' lab |url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2021/12/07/metro/lawsuit-alleges-mit-professor-groomed-young-women-ran-sexually-charged-lab/ |work=The Boston Globe |date=December 7, 2021 |access-date=October 30, 2026}}</ref>

A separate [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] investigation found that Sabatini had violated its policy on sexual relationships with people over whom faculty held a career-influencing role. He resigned his tenured professorship in April 2022 after officials recommended revoking his tenure.<ref name="science2022">{{cite news |last=Wadman |first=Meredith |title=Prominent biologist David Sabatini out at MIT after breaching sexual relationship policy |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/prominent-biologist-david-sabatini-out-mit-after-breaching-sexual-relationship-policy |work=Science |publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science |date=April 1, 2022}}</ref> In May, he withdrew from consideration for a position at [[NYU Langone Health|NYU Langone]] following student and faculty protests.<ref name="nytimes">{{cite news |last=Wong |first=Ashley |title=N.Y.U. Will Not Hire Scientist Accused of Harassment After Backlash |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/05/03/nyregion/david-sabatini-nyu-harassment.html |work=The New York Times |date=May 3, 2022}}</ref>

In November 2025, the court dismissed Sabatini's remaining gender-discrimination claim against Whitehead and Lehmann and narrowed his claims against Knouse, allowing [[defamation]] and [[tortious interference|tortious-interference]] claims to proceed.<ref name="Murphy-2025"/>

On October 16, 2026, a [[Suffolk County, Massachusetts|Suffolk County]] jury found Knouse liable for defamation and tortious interference and awarded Sabatini $6 million plus interest.<ref name="Globe-verdict-2026">{{cite news |last1=Swearing |first1=Madyline |last2=Hecht |first2=Bryan |last3=Alanez |first3=Tonya |title=Jury rules in favor of ousted Cambridge scientist David Sabatini, with $6 million in damages to be awarded |url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/10/16/metro/david-sabatini-verdict/ |work=The Boston Globe |date=October 16, 2026 |access-date=October 30, 2026}}</ref> It also rejected all of Knouse's counterclaims, including sexual harassment and retaliation.<ref name="Arsenault-2026-verdict">{{cite news |last=Arsenault |first=Mark |title=M.I.T. Scientist Wins $6 Million in Sexual Harassment Defamation Suit |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/us/mit-scientist-sexual-harassment-defamation-lawsuit-david-sabatini.html |work=The New York Times |date=October 16, 2026 |access-date=October 30, 2026}}</ref> ''[[The Boston Globe]]'' described the verdict as a "stark rejection of a high-profile [[MeToo movement|#MeToo]] claim" from Knouse.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Swearing |first1=Madyline |last2=Hecht|first2=Bryan | last3=Alanez|first3=Tonya |date=October 16, 2026 |title=David Sabatini lawsuit ends with $6 million defamation verdict |url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/10/16/metro/david-sabatini-verdict/ |access-date=October 17, 2026 |work=The Boston Globe |language=en-US |issn=0743-1791}}</ref>

===Independent funding and IOCB Prague===
In February 2023, [[Bill Ackman]] and an unnamed partner announced $25 million to fund Sabatini's research, though it is unclear if he could successfully find an institution willing to host his lab or if one could be built independently.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2023/02/07/metro/new-funding-controversial-mit-whitehead-institute-scientist-david-sabatini-draws-divided-reactions/ |title=New funding for controversial MIT and Whitehead Institute scientist David Sabatini draws divided reactions|last=Arsenault|first=Mark|date=February 7, 2023|work=The Boston Globe|access-date=February 19, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=David Sabatini, biologist fired for sexual misconduct, lands millions from private donors to start new lab|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/sabatini-biologist-fired-sexual-misconduct-lands-millions-private-donors-start-new-lab|last=Wadman|first=Meredith|date=February 3, 2023|access-date=February 19, 2023|work=Science|publisher= American Association for the Advancement of Science}}</ref> By November 2023, Sabatini had accepted a position at the [[Institute of Organic Chemistry and Biochemistry]] (IOCB) of the [[Czech Academy of Sciences]] in [[Prague]],<ref>{{cite news|last=Arsenault|first=Mark|date=November 13, 2023|title=Former MIT biologist, who lost positions after engaging in a prohibited sexual relationship, accepts new science position in Prague|work=The Boston Globe|url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2023/11/13/metro/former-mit-biologist-david-sabatini-ousted-after-prohibited-sexual-relationship-accepts-new-science-position-prague/|access-date=November 13, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Despite sexual harassment shadow, biologist David Sabatini lands job at top Czech institute|last=Wadman|first=Meredith|date=November 13, 2023|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/despite-sexual-harassment-shadow-biologist-david-sabatini-lands-job-top-czech-institute|access-date=November 18, 2023| work=Science|publisher= American Association for the Advancement of Science}}</ref> and in April 2024 it was announced that IOCB would open a Boston branch, where it was planned that Sabatini would spend part of his time.<ref>{{cite news|title= Former MIT biologist David Sabatini, forced out after sexual harassment accusations, to lead new Boston team |last=Arsenault | first=Mark|work=The Boston Globe|url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2024/04/30/metro/david-sabatini-to-open-boston-lab/|date=April 30, 2024|access-date=May 3, 2024}}</ref> His lab now has two physical locations, one in Prague and the other in Boston (IOCB – Boston).{{cn|date=April 2025}}

==Scientific contributions==
As a graduate student in [[Solomon H. Snyder]]'s lab at Johns Hopkins, Sabatini began working on understanding the molecular mechanism of [[rapamycin]]; a macrolide antibiotic discovered in the soil of [[Easter Island]] that has potent antifungal, immunosuppressive, and anti-tumorigenic properties.<ref name="Viegas-2017">{{Cite journal|last=Viegas|first=Jennifer|date=December 26, 2017|title=Profile of David M. Sabatini|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|volume=115|issue=3|pages=438–440|pmc=5777013|doi=10.1073/pnas.1721196115|pmid=29279397|doi-access=free}}</ref> Although the TOR/DRR genes had been identified in 1993 as conferring rapamycin resistance in [[budding yeast]], the direct target of rapamycin and its mechanism of action in mammals was unknown.<ref name="pmid8387896">{{cite journal |vauthors=Kunz J, Henriquez R, Schneider U, Deuter-Reinhard M, Movva NR, Hall MN |title=Target of rapamycin in yeast, TOR2, is an essential phosphatidylinositol kinase homolog required for G1 progression |journal=Cell |volume=73 |issue=3 |pages=585–96 |year=1993 |pmid=8387896 |doi= 10.1016/0092-8674(93)90144-f|s2cid=42926249 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Cafferkey R, Young PR, McLaughlin MM, Bergsma DJ, Koltin Y, Sathe GM, Faucette L, Eng WK, Johnson RK, Livi GP |title=Dominant missense mutations in a novel yeast protein related to mammalian phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase and VPS34 abrogate rapamycin cytotoxicity |journal=Mol. Cell. Biol. |volume=13 |issue=10 |pages=6012–23 |year=1993 |pmid=8413204 |pmc=364661 |doi= 10.1128/mcb.13.10.6012}}</ref> In 1994, Sabatini used rapamycin and its binding partner [[FKBP12]] to purify the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) protein from rat brain, showing it to be the direct target of rapamycin in mammals and the homolog of the yeast TOR/DRR genes.<ref name="Viegas-2017" />

Since starting his own lab at the Whitehead Institute in 1997, Sabatini has made numerous key contributions to the understanding of mTOR function, regulation, and importance in diseases such as [[cancer]].<ref name="pmid28388417">{{cite journal |vauthors=Saxton RA, Sabatini, DM |title= mTOR Signaling in Growth, Metabolism, and Disease |journal=Cell |volume=169 |issue=2 |pages=361–371 |year=2017 |pmid=28388417 |doi= 10.1016/j.cell.2017.03.035|doi-access=free |hdl=1721.1/116766 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> For example, his lab discovered the [[mTORC1]]<ref name="pmid12150925">{{cite journal |vauthors=Kim DH, Sarbassov DD, Ali SM, et al. |title=mTOR interacts with raptor to form a nutrient-sensitive complex that signals to the cell growth machinery |journal=Cell |volume=110 |issue=2 |pages=163–75 |year=2002 |pmid=12150925 |doi= 10.1016/s0092-8674(02)00808-5|s2cid=4656930 |doi-access=free }}</ref> and [[mTORC2]]<ref name="pmid15268862">{{cite journal |vauthors=Sarbassov DD, Ali SM, Kim DH, et al. |title=Rictor, a novel binding partner of mTOR, defines a rapamycin-insensitive and raptor-independent pathway that regulates the cytoskeleton |journal=Curr. Biol. |volume=14 |issue=14 |pages=1296–302 |year=2004 |pmid=15268862 |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2004.06.054 |s2cid=4658268 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2004CBio...14.1296D }}</ref> multi-protein complexes, the nutrient sensing Rag GTPase pathway upstream of mTORC1,<ref name="pmid18497260">{{cite journal |vauthors=Sancak Y, Peterson TR, Shaul YD, et al. |title=The Rag GTPases bind raptor and mediate amino acid signaling to mTORC1 |journal=Science |volume=320 |issue=5882 |pages=1496–501 |year=2008 |pmid=18497260 |pmc=2475333 |doi=10.1126/science.1157535 |bibcode=2008Sci...320.1496S }}</ref> as well as the direct amino acid sensors Sestrin<ref name="pmid26449471">{{cite journal |vauthors=Wolfson RL, Chantranupong L, Saxton RA, et al. |title=Sestrin2 is a leucine sensor for the mTORC1 pathway |journal=Science |volume=351 |issue=6268 |pages=43–8 |year=2016 |pmid=26449471 |pmc=4698017 |doi=10.1126/science.aab2674 |bibcode=2016Sci...351...43W }}</ref><ref name="pmid26586190">{{cite journal |vauthors=Saxton RA, Knockenhauer KE, Wolfson RL, et al. |title=Structural basis for leucine sensing by the Sestrin2-mTORC1 pathway |journal=Science |volume=351 |issue=6268 |pages=53–8 |year=2016 |pmid=26586190 |pmc=4698039 |doi=10.1126/science.aad2087 |bibcode=2016Sci...351...53S }}</ref> and CASTOR.<ref name="pmid26972053">{{cite journal |vauthors=Chantranupong L, Scaria SM, Saxton RA, et al. |title=The CASTOR Proteins Are Arginine Sensors for the mTORC1 Pathway |journal=Cell |volume=165 |issue=1 |pages=153–64 |year=2016 |pmid=26972053 |pmc=4808398 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2016.02.035 }}</ref><ref name="pmid27487210">{{cite journal |vauthors=Saxton RA, Chantranupong L, Knockenhauer KE, Schwartz TU, Sabatini DM |title=Mechanism of arginine sensing by CASTOR1 upstream of mTORC1 |journal=Nature |volume=536 |issue=7615 |pages=229–33 |year=2016 |pmid=27487210 |doi=10.1038/nature19079 |pmc=4988899 |bibcode=2016Natur.536..229S }}</ref>
 
[[Image:MTOR-pathway-v1.7.svg|thumb|right|300px|mTOR signaling pathway]]

Sabatini's research interests have expanded in recent years to include cancer metabolism as well as technology development surrounding the use of high-throughput genetic screens in human cells, most notably through the use of [[RNA interference]]<ref name="pmid16564017">{{cite journal |vauthors=Moffat J, Grueneberg DA, Yang X, et al. |title=A lentiviral RNAi library for human and mouse genes applied to an arrayed viral high-content screen |journal=Cell |volume=124 |issue=6 |pages=1283–98 |year=2006 |pmid=16564017 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2006.01.040 |s2cid=630641 |doi-access=free }}</ref> and the [[CRISPR|CRISPR-Cas9 system]].<ref name="pmid24336569">{{cite journal |vauthors=Wang T, Wei JJ, Sabatini DM, Lander ES |title=Genetic screens in human cells using the CRISPR-Cas9 system |journal=Science |volume=343 |issue=6166 |pages=80–4 |year=2014 |pmid=24336569 |pmc=3972032 |doi=10.1126/science.1246981 |url=https://dspace.mit.edu/bitstream/1721.1/96677/1/Lander_Genetic%20screens.pdf|bibcode=2014Sci...343...80W }}</ref>
